notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Malachi 3, drawn from the sources available.

---

## Malachi 3:1 — The Two Messengers

**Traditional Reading (all major Protestant traditions):** The "first messenger" is John the Baptist. The "second messenger" — the "Lord" who comes to His temple and the "Messenger of the covenant" — is Jesus Christ Himself.

- David Guzik (Enduring Word): "This prophesied messenger is none other than John the Baptist. Matthew 11:10, Mark 1:2, and Luke 7:27 all show this promise was fulfilled in John the Baptist." The second messenger is "Jesus coming to His temple as the fulfillment of the old covenant and to institute a new covenant." The imagery of "prepare the way" comes from ancient royal processions, where a messenger went before the king to announce his arrival and remove obstacles. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- John Gill: The words "are the words of Christ, in answer to the question … 'Where is the God of judgment?'" The first messenger is John the Baptist — "not by nature, but by office; and Christ's messenger, because sent by him." This proves "the proper deity of Christ" since John was sent by Him before the incarnation. The second is "the Lord, whom ye seek … the Son of God, and promised Messiah." He comes "suddenly … to his temple — meaning not his human nature, nor his church … but the material temple at Jerusalem, the second temple." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

- Charles Ellicott: The first messenger "by the distinct reference to Isaiah 40:3 … is evidently the same as he whom [the deutero-] Isaiah prophetically heard crying, 'In the wilderness, prepare ye the way of the LORD.'" Identified with the "Elijah" of Malachi 4:5, and "had their first, if not their perfect fulfilment in John the Baptist." The second messenger, "the messenger of the covenant" — "Identified as He is here with 'the Lord,' He can be no other than the Son of God, who was manifested in the flesh as the Messiah." The term "covenant" may reference the "new covenant" (Jeremiah 31:31), but should not be limited to that. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- Precept Austin (citing John Piper): Notes three individuals in the verse: (1) "I" — Jehovah/the Father speaking; (2) "my messenger" — John the Baptist, the Elijah-like forerunner; (3) "the Lord … the messenger of the covenant" — the divine Son of God. Piper argues the third is divine because He is called "Lord," the temple is "His," and He seems interchangeable with "Me" (Jehovah) in the first half of the verse. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_3_commentary)

- Geneva Study Bible (Reformed): The first messenger "is meant of John the Baptist, as Christ interprets it; Lu 7:27." The second is "Christ, by whom the covenant was made and ratified, who is called the angel or messenger of the covenant, because he reconciles us to his Father." (From search excerpt, studylight.org)

- Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: The first messenger is John the Baptist; "the sudden coming of the Lord to His temple alludes to His second coming, when He shall come in power and expansive glory." Jesus is "the messenger of the covenant, the one whom all prophecy had presented and God had promised as the Redeemer." (From search excerpt, studylight.org)

**Catholic Reading:**

- Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org): "The Lord is here identified with the angel of the testament; this is evident from the construction of the phrase and from the circumstance that the description of the mission of the angel of the testament (vv. 2 sq.) is continued by the Lord speaking of Himself in the first person in v. 5." The New Testament "categorically interpret this double prophecy by applying to John the Baptist, precursor of our Lord (Matthew 11:10, 14; 17:11-12)." (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09562b.htm)

**Modern Scholarship / Other Views:**

- Layman's Bible Commentary: "The problem of the identity of the messenger and of his relationship to the Lord has vexed interpreters from the time of the editor of the book to the present day." The editor may have thought Malachi himself was the messenger; an annotator (Mal 4:5) thought Elijah. Mark and the early church identified John the Baptist. "It is probable that the writer of the prophecy thought only of the messenger who announced the coming of a royal personage … The messenger is thus an agent, representing the coming of the Lord to his Temple, rather than a particular historical person." Malachi "may have expected a priest to accomplish the reformation in the Temple." Further: "the traditional Davidic Messianic figure does not appear; instead, the direct intervention of the Lord himself is all that can be seen." (From search excerpt, studylight.org)

---

## Malachi 3:2 — Who Can Endure the Day of His Coming?

**Traditional Reading:** The coming of the Lord will be fearful — not to destroy but to purify, like a refiner's fire and launderer's soap.

- David Guzik: "The coming that man must endure is the coming of the Messenger of the covenant, but it is His second coming." Like most OT prophets, Malachi "mingled the two advents." Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "If any of you, my hearers, are seeking the Lord … you are seeking a fire which will test you, and consume much which has been dear to you." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- John Gill: The "day of his coming" refers to when Christ would "be manifest in Israel, and come preaching the Gospel" — "who could bear the doctrines delivered by him … concerning his deity and equality with God the Father … especially since for judgment he came?" Also includes the judgment at Jerusalem's destruction. The "refiner's fire" is partly the ministry of the Word (Jer 23:29) separating pure from dross doctrines, and partly His "fiery dispensations and judgments on the wicked Jews." The "fuller's soap" likewise signifies removing spotted doctrines and persons. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

- Charles Ellicott: "This coming of the Lord to His temple acts as a crucial test (comp. Luke 2:35); the people ought, therefore, seriously to have considered how far they were prepared for that advent before they desired it so eagerly and impatiently." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: "Who may abide or stand in the day of His coming, His coming in judgment, a thing the priests had actually questioned, Malachi 2:17 … The answer is that none shall stand, but all shall bow to the penalties of unforgiven sins." (From search excerpt, studylight.org)

---

## Malachi 3:3 — He Will Sit as a Refiner and Purifier

**Traditional Reading:** Christ Himself, with patient care, purifies His people — beginning with the priesthood ("sons of Levi") — so that they can offer acceptable worship. The image of sitting suggests careful, patient work.

- David Guzik: "He will sit as a refiner" — "The beauty of this picture is that the refiner looks into the open furnace … and knows that the process of purifying is complete … when he can see his image plainly reflected in the molten metal" (citing Baldwin). The sitting posture "shows that the refiner may seem indifferent, but He is not. He is carefully working with the silver, burning off and scraping away the dross." Guzik also quotes Spurgeon rejecting any notion of purgatory: "When Christ's refining work is done upon us there will never be any need for it again … there is no purgatorial fire." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- John Gill: "Maimonides understands the passage of the Messiah." Christ "sitting, while his people are purifying and refining … denotes the continued care of Christ over them; his eye is upon them, that nothing be lost but their dross and corruption." The "sons of Levi" refers literally to priests, some of whom were converted (Acts 6:7), or figuratively to all believers as a royal priesthood. Both are purified "by his blood, and the imputation of his righteousness … and by the Spirit in sanctification." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

- Charles Ellicott: "'Sons of Levi' — meaning especially the priests … for judgment must begin at the house of God (comp. 1 Peter 4:17). 'In righteousness' refers rather to the moral character of the offerer than to the nature of the sacrifices." Ellicott adds that this verse does "not, of course, imply that there are to be material sacrifices in Messianic times. The prophet speaks in such language as was suitable to the age in which he lived." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- Geneva Study Bible (Reformed): "He begins at the priests, that they might be lights, and shine unto others." (From search excerpt)

---

## Malachi 3:4 — Offerings Pleasing to the Lord

**Traditional Reading:** After purification, the worship of God's people will once again be pleasing to Him, as in the idealized early days (patriarchal/Mosaic era).

- Charles Ellicott: "'Days of old … former years' — perhaps … from the time of Moses to the first year of the reign of Solomon. But we cannot be certain." He notes a characteristic of Malachi is to be "somewhat of a laudator temporis acti" (a praiser of times past). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- John Gill: "as in the days of old, and as in former years: under the first temple, and when the tabernacle was set up by Moses, and in the times of the patriarchs; and even before the flood, and as early as Abel, who offered a more excellent sacrifice than Cain." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

- Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: "This seems to refer to the time of restoration of the morning and evening oblation sacrifices for a period of about 3½ years … immediately preceding the coming of our Lord in the air" — a dispensational, futurist reading linking to Daniel 9 and Revelation 11. (From search excerpt)

**Catholic Reading:**

- Catholic Encyclopedia: Regarding Malachi 1:11 (the "pure offering" from east to west), the Council of Trent (Session XXII, 1) understood it as a prophecy of the Eucharistic sacrifice. This shapes the Catholic reading of Malachi's purification-of-worship theme as pointing toward the Mass. (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09562b.htm)

- Layman's Bible Commentary notes that "Protestant scholars deny the Roman Catholic view that this prophesies the establishment of the Mass, but they have provided little constructive interpretation to take the place of this idea." (From search excerpt, studylight.org)

---

## Malachi 3:5 — Swift Witness Against Sinners

**Traditional Reading:** God will draw near for judgment against specific sins — sorcery, adultery, perjury, oppression of the vulnerable, and injustice to foreigners. All these were explicitly forbidden in the Law.

- Charles Ellicott: Lists the specific Old Testament prohibitions behind each sin mentioned: sorcery (Ex 22:18), adultery (Ex 20:14; Lev 20:10; Deut 22:22), false swearing (Lev 19:12), defrauding wages (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14-15), oppressing widow/orphan (Ex 22:22-24), injustice to stranger (Deut 24:17; 27:19). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- John Gill: Notes that "sorcerers" are mentioned first "because there were many that used the magic art … in the age of Christ and his apostles, even many of their doctors and members of the sanhedrim." The root of all the sins is "fear not me, saith the Lord of hosts — irreverence of Christ, disbelief of him, and contempt of his Gospel." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

- David Guzik: "When Jesus returns in glory and rules on this earth, evil will be quickly punished. Sorcerers: This sin is mentioned first because the Jews became familiar with sorcery and other magical arts during their captivity in Babylon." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

---

## Malachi 3:6 — "I the LORD Do Not Change"

**Traditional Reading:** God's unchanging nature is the reason Israel has not been destroyed despite her sins. His covenant faithfulness preserves them.

- Charles Ellicott: "For I Jehovah change not. Because it is the Eternal's unchangeable will that the sons of Jacob, His chosen people, should not perish as a nation, He will purify them by the eradication of the wicked among them, that the remnant … may return to their allegiance. (Comp. Romans 11)." Ellicott rejects Ewald's alternative rendering ("have ye not altered?"), saying the verb does not mean "to alter" and the traditional translation matches Ezra 9:14-15. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- David Guzik: "If it were possible for God to change His mind about us, He might very well do it and we would be consumed. Fortunately, the LORD does not change in His love for us or His choice of us." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- John Gill: This is "a proof of the deity of Christ, who here speaks." "He changed not in his divine nature and personality by becoming man … nor did he change in his threatenings of destruction to the Jews … nor in his promises … nor will he ever change in his love and affections to them." The "sons of Jacob" not consumed are "such who were Israelites indeed, true believers in Christ; these were not consumed when the wicked Jews were, but were directed to leave the city before its destruction." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

---

## Malachi 3:7 — "Return to Me, and I Will Return to You"

**Traditional Reading:** A simple call to repentance, met with feigned innocence — "How shall we return?"

- David Guzik: "In its most basic sense, repentance is turning away from sin and turning to God. It isn't so much required if we want to return to God; repentance describes what the very act of returning is." Israel "didn't know how to return to God. Either they chose not to know, or they simply were ignorant." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- John Gill: "This message was carried to them by John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ, and by Christ himself, who both preached the doctrine of repentance to this people." Their question "Wherein shall we return?" is "the true language of the Pharisees in Christ's time, who, touching the righteousness of the law, were blameless in their own esteem, and were the ninety and nine just persons that needed not repentance, Luke 15:7." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

- Charles Ellicott: "Throughout the whole course of their history they had been a people (Exodus 32:9, &c.); and now, when exhorted to repent, they ask in feigned innocence: 'Wherein shall we return?'" Cites Zechariah 1:3 for the same pattern. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

---

## Malachi 3:8–9 — Robbing God in Tithes and Offerings

**Traditional Reading:** Withholding the full tithe is "robbing God." This is because the tithe was specifically devoted to Him and His house; failing to give it brought a curse.

- David Guzik: God called it robbery "because they had unlawful possession of what belonged to God." While everything belongs to God (Ps 24:1), "the tithes and offerings are different; they are not given to us to manage — they belong to what the LORD calls My house." The Law of Moses had a detailed tithing system (Deut 14:22-29) with a 20% penalty for non-payment (Lev 5:14-16). Yet "the practice and principle of tithing came long before the law (Genesis 14:18-20)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- John Gill: The Hebrew can be read "Will a man rob God? or 'the gods'; the false gods, the idols of the Gentiles; the Heathens will not do that, accounting sacrilege a great sin, and yet this the Jews were guilty of." Also notes the alternative "or 'the judges' … civil magistrates." The robbery is "keeping back from the priests and Levites, his ministers, what was due to them." Gill notes a possible objection — that Jews in Christ's time did pay tithes (Matt 23:23) — but replies they did so "with an evil eye … grudgingly … and with an evil intention … in order to merit at his hands." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

- Charles Ellicott: "Robbed me. — Because the tithes are said to be offered to Jehovah, and then He gives them to the Levites in place of an inheritance (Numbers 18:24)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- John Wesley (Methodist): "Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me." (From search excerpt, biblehub.com/wes)

- Benson's Commentary (Methodist/Holiness): Emphasizes that this was a call to "repentance, and amendment of life." (From search excerpt, studylight.org)

---

## Malachi 3:10–12 — "Bring the Full Tithe … Test Me in This"

**This is the passage where Protestant traditions most clearly diverge, particularly on whether the tithe is binding on New Covenant believers and whether the promised blessings are material/financial.**

**Traditional Evangelical / "Tithing Is a Continuing Principle" View:**

- David Guzik (broad evangelical): Emphasizes that the NT "nowhere specifically commands tithing, but it certainly does speak of it in a positive light if it is done with a right heart (Luke 11:42)." Tithing "is not a principle that depends on the Law of Moses … Hebrews 7:5-9 explains that tithing was practiced and honored by God long before the Law of Moses." However, the NT emphasizes principles of giving: periodic, planned, proportional, private, generous, freely given, and cheerful (1 Cor 16:1-4; 2 Cor 9). "Since the New Testament doesn't emphasize tithing, one might not be strict on it for Christians … Nevertheless, because giving is to be proportional, we should give some percentage, and ten percent is a good benchmark. For some people, 10% should really be the beginning of their giving." Guzik adds: "If our question is, 'How little can I give and still please God?' then our heart isn't in the right place at all." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

**Prosperity / Word of Faith Use (widely noted but not endorsed in the scholarly commentaries examined):**

- While none of the traditional commentaries reviewed promote prosperity teaching, Guzik notes that "Try Me now in this" is "hard to find a comparable passage of Scripture — where the LORD commanded His people to test Him." He quotes Boice: "The context for God's words about tithes is the teaching that God is faithful. The matter of tithes is only an illustration of that teaching." The "windows of heaven" reference "reminds us of the glorious account of provision in 2 Kings 7, when God provided in a completely unexpected way. God has resources that we know nothing about." Guzik sees this as about provision and protection, not a "get rich" formula. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

**Dispensational / Baptist Views:**

- Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: "Non-payment of tithes brought national calamity on Israel" — framing tithing within Israel's national covenant rather than directly applying to the church. (From search excerpt, studylight.org)

**On the Storehouse and the Promise:**

- Charles Ellicott: "The emphasis is on the word 'all.'" The "storehouse" — "From the time of Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 31:11) there were at the Sanctuary special storehouses built for this purpose; so, too, in the second Temple (Nehemiah 10:38-39)." "Meat — i.e., food for the priests and Levites." On the blessing: "There shall not be room enough … This rendering gives the correct meaning of the words (Compare an expression of similar import in Zechariah 10:10.) We cannot agree with the rendering of Gesenius, 'until my abundance be exhausted,' as equivalent to 'for ever.'" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- On the "devourer" (v. 11): Ellicott identifies it as "the locust, &c." He notes the verb "rebuke" is the same word as Malachi 2:3 but in a good sense here. The vine not casting "her fruit before the time" refers to crop failure. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

---

## Malachi 3:13–15 — "It Is Futile to Serve God"

**Traditional Reading:** The people accused God of injustice — the proud and wicked prosper while the faithful suffer. This was "harsh" speech against the Lord, rooted in outward religiosity that expected material reward.

- Charles Ellicott: The people's words "put a constraint on me: viz., to prove myself to you to be 'the God of judgment.'" They were in the habit of "conversing together, and comparing the promises of God towards them with the then state of affairs." Ellicott sees in v. 14 "that disposition to attribute merit to observances of outward forms of religion for their own sake … which reached such a pitch among the majority of the Jews in the time of our Lord, and especially among the Pharisees." In v. 15 he observes "the seeds of sceptical Sadduceism, as in Malachi 3:14 of hypocritical Phariseism." The "proud" are "the heathen, who do not profess to serve Jehovah." Their "tempting" of God is different from the faithful testing in v. 10: "In Malachi 3:10 the Jews are exhorted to obey the Law faithfully, and prove whether God would not perform His part … In Malachi 3:15 the heathen, by their pride and wickedness, tempt God to judgment." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- David Guzik: "They saw the prosperity of the proud and those who did wickedness, and they felt that it was useless to serve God as long as those who didn't serve Him seemed to live comfortably. It cost something to keep God's ordinance, and they had to humble themselves to walk as mourners before the LORD. Yet it seemed to God's people that the cost wasn't worth the reward." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

---

## Malachi 3:16 — The Book of Remembrance

**Traditional Reading:** In response to the cynical talk of the unfaithful, the faithful remnant spoke together and encouraged one another in the Lord. God heard, and He recorded their faithfulness in a "book of remembrance."

- David Guzik: "Discouraged by the sense that it wasn't worth the trouble to serve God, the people of God came together — spoke to one another — and encouraged each other in the LORD. When God's people speak to one another in this way, the LORD listens from heaven. He loves to see true fellowship and love among His people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- Charles Ellicott: "As a consequence of the unbelieving conversation of the wicked … they strengthened one another in their faith and reliance on the goodness and faithfulness of the Lord, in spite of the present appearance of things." The "book of remembrance" is figurative language — "In which men's actions are said figuratively to be recorded (Psalm 56:8; Daniel 7:10, &c.). Compare the custom of the Persian kings (Esther 6:1)." The phrase "thought upon his name" means "valued, esteemed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- John Gill (implied by his introduction): Those who feared the Lord were "taken notice of by him, and were dear unto him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

- Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: "Those, who in the midst of the disparaging wickedness, feared the Lord, and spake often or fellowshipped one with another, were observed of the Lord … What is more He recorded, in a book of remembrance, the deeds of those who feared Him … as a Persian king kept record and rewarded those of merit in his kingdom." (From search excerpt, studylight.org)

---

## Malachi 3:17 — "My Treasured Possession … I Will Spare Them"

**Traditional Reading:** God claims the faithful remnant as His own special possession ("jewels"), and promises to spare them as a father spares an obedient son — a promise of eschatological salvation.

- David Guzik: "In the midst of suffering, assaulted by doubt and discouragement, God's people didn't feel like God's jewels. Yet their feelings didn't change the fact." Lists several ways believers are like jewels: hard and durable, prized for luster, rare, made by God alone, of all different sizes, found worldwide, associated with royalty, protected, some hidden, some not yet polished. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- Charles Ellicott: "Better, And they shall be to me, saith the Lord of hosts, a special possession, on the day that I am about to make." The phrase "special possession" references Exodus 19:5. The "day … make" is the same expression used in Malachi 4:3 (the coming Day of the Lord). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

---

## Malachi 3:18 — Distinguishing Righteous from Wicked

**Traditional Reading:** On the day of the Lord, the distinction between those who serve God and those who do not will be made unmistakably clear — resolving the painful question of why the wicked seem to prosper.

- David Guzik: "One day this dilemma will be cleared up. In the end, the distinction between the righteous and the wicked will be evident." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-3/)

- Charles Ellicott: "Better, Then shall ye again perceive the difference between. For the construction, comp. Zechariah 4:1. As in former cases God had made this difference manifest, so He would again. Compare, for instance, the difference between the case of the Egyptians and of the Israelites in the matter of the miraculous darkness (Exodus 10:23)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/malachi/3.htm)

- John Gill: "The time would come when there would be a manifest difference made between the one and the other." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/malachi/3.htm)

---

## Summary of Where Traditions Diverge

1. **First vs. Second Coming (vv. 1–5):** Most traditional commentators (Gill, Guzik, Ellicott, Geneva Bible) see a blending of both advents. Baptist commentator Garner-Howes specifically references the Second Coming for vv. 1–2 and links v. 4 to a future Tribulation-era restoration of sacrifices. Guzik also leans toward Second Coming for the judgment aspect. Gill uniquely applies vv. 2–3 to Christ's first advent ministry and the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

2. **Tithing (vv. 8–12):** The sharpest practical divide. Guzik represents the common evangelical view: the tithe principle predates the Law (Abraham) and remains a good benchmark, but NT giving principles supersede a strict 10% command. The Garner-Howes Baptist commentary frames tithing within Israel's national covenant. Prosperity/Word of Faith teachers (not represented in the traditional commentaries examined) are widely known to use Mal 3:10 as a proof-text for "testing God" with money to receive material wealth — but this was not found endorsed in any of the sources.

3. **Eucharistic Sacrifice (Catholic reading of vv. 3–4):** The Catholic Encyclopedia and Council of Trent see Malachi's promise of a restored, pure, universal offering as a prophecy of the Mass. Protestant commentaries explicitly reject this, seeing the passage as about purified spiritual worship under both old and new covenants, or a future millennial restoration.

4. **Identity of the "Sons of Levi" (v. 3):** Gill and others see this figuratively as all believers (the priesthood of all believers). Ellicott and the Geneva Bible take it more literally as the priests who needed reformation. Garner-Howes applies it to Levites purified through trial for their specific sins (divorce, foreign wives).
